paragraphs.heading: What it counts
paragraphs.text: For a given whole number n, Euler's totient function counts how many of the numbers from 1 to n are relatively prime to n, meaning their greatest common divisor with n is 1. It is written with the Greek letter phi, as φ(n), and is also called Euler's phi function. The numbers it counts are sometimes called the totatives of n.

paragraphs.heading: Two small examples
paragraphs.text: Take n = 9. Of the numbers 1 to 9, six are relatively prime to it: 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 and 8. The remaining three, 3, 6 and 9, fail: their greatest common divisor with 9 is 3 for the first two and 9 for the last. At the other extreme, φ(1) = 1, because 1 is the only number in range and gcd(1, 1) = 1.

paragraphs.heading: Counting for twenty
paragraphs.text: For n = 20, the distinct prime factors are 2 and 5. Half of the numbers 1 to 20 are even, which leaves ten; a fifth of those ten are multiples of 5, which leaves eight. Those eight, 1, 3, 7, 9, 11, 13, 17 and 19, are the ones relatively prime to 20. A formula that uses only whole numbers, built from the prime factors 2² and 5¹, gives the same count, since 2⋅1⋅1⋅4 = 8.

paragraphs.heading: Multiplying
paragraphs.text: The function is multiplicative: when m and n are relatively prime, φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n). One way to see this uses the Chinese remainder theorem. It matches each pair made of one number counted for m and one counted for n with exactly one number counted for mn.

paragraphs.heading: History and name
paragraphs.text: Leonhard Euler introduced the function in 1763 but gave it no symbol at the time. In a 1784 publication he studied it further and used the Greek letter π for it. The symbol φ used today comes from Gauss's 1801 treatise Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, though Gauss wrote φA without parentheses. The name totient was coined by Sylvester.

paragraphs.heading: Groups and secret codes
paragraphs.text: For the multiplicative group of integers modulo n, φ(n) gives the order of that group. It is also used to define the RSA encryption system. In RSA, the private decryption exponent d is the multiplicative inverse of the public encryption exponent e modulo φ(n). The private key holder builds n by multiplying two large, randomly chosen primes p and q, and so knows its factors. Only n is made public, and because large numbers are hard to factor, nobody else knows them.
